items.title: Generating running routes with GPT-6 Astra and ChatGPT Work
items.one_liner: An AI agent successfully generated localized running routes using OpenStreetMap data, but opaque chat thread compaction blocked access to its underlying Python execution code.
items.summary: Simon Willison used GPT-6 Astra (Max) via ChatGPT Work to successfully generate 5K and 10K running routes looping from his home using OpenStreetMap data via Nominatim and Overpass. The tool ran for 27 minutes and produced embedded visualizations alongside downloadable GPX and GeoJSON files. However, thread compaction in the ChatGPT UI prevented him from retrieving the underlying Python code that the agent had executed, highlighting a lack of execution transparency. The generated maps utilized D3 loaded from an allow-listed CDN supported by the system's visualize skill.
items.bottom_line: AI agent tools that rely on automatic thread compaction must preserve pre-compacted text and expose it via tool calls to maintain execution transparency.

items.title: OpenClaw went viral. Meet the maintainers building and securing it.
items.one_liner: OpenClaw maintainers discuss managing thousands of AI-generated pull requests, contributor trust, and securing a viral open source project.
items.summary: OpenClaw creator Peter Steinberger and project maintainers discuss the rapid growth and security challenges of the personal AI assistant project in a video interview. Started in November 2025, the repository expanded to roughly 388,000 stars, 81,000 forks, and over 80,000 commits by August 2026. The maintainers highlight how automated contributor tools flooded the project with hundreds of simulated pull requests, shifting the core challenge from attracting participation to filtering high-volume noise. They also share strategies for welcoming non-developer contributors who utilize AI agents, balancing work-life boundaries, and implementing security baselines learned through the GitHub Secure Open Source Fund.
items.bottom_line: Viral open source projects driven by AI tooling face unprecedented pull request floods that require automated filtering and robust contributor governance.

items.summary: TL;DR CVE-2026-58073 (CVSS 9.5) and CVE-2026-58072 (CVSS 9.0) are critical vulnerabilities in Veeam Service Provider Console, the multi-tenant console that managed service providers use to run backups across all of their customers. The first lets an unauthenticated network peer claim a connected backup agent’s identity and receive that agent’s real certificate. The second lets anything holding an agent certificate write a file anywhere on the server. Chained, they are unauthenticated remote code execution on the console that sits above every tenant’s backups, which we proved end to end against Veeam’s own binaries. Patch to 9.3.0, then check your logs for indicators of compromise.

items.title: Old Census town criteria will not capture India’s urbanisation, Ministry tells House panel
items.one_liner: The Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs warns Parliament that 1981 Census Town criteria drastically underestimate India's true urbanisation.
items.summary: The Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA) informed a parliamentary committee that India's four-decade-old Census Town criteria fail to capture the actual scale of urbanisation. The rigid definition, established in 1981, relies on parameters such as a minimum population of 5,000, a population density of 400 persons per square kilometer, and a requirement that 75% of male working populations engage in non-agricultural work. MoHUA criticized the definition for ignoring peri-urban growth, utilizing a flawed male-biased workforce metric, and relying on administrative rather than built-up boundaries. Although the Registrar General of India maintained that altering the framework for Census 2027 is unfeasible, policy advisors note that actual urbanization may significantly exceed official estimates.
items.bottom_line: India's outdated 1981 rural-urban classification criteria fail to capture modern economic transformations, though the Registrar General of India declined changes for the upcoming census.

items.title: Execution Flexibility in Automated Planning: A Comparative Evaluation of Deordering and Reordering Strategies
items.one_liner: Block deordering strategies outperform MaxSAT approaches for enhancing automated plan execution flexibility.
items.summary: This research study evaluates strategies for enhancing plan-execution flexibility in automated planning by comparing deordering and reordering approaches. The central finding indicates that block deordering-based methods substantially outperform MaxSAT-based approaches by restructuring causal dependencies through block-level grouping and subplan substitution. Unlike MaxSAT methods that optimize within existing causal structures and fail entirely on a substantial portion of plans, block deordering functions as an anytime algorithm that yields valid results efficiently. Block substitution further aids parallel execution constraints, achieving higher flexibility gains per unit of computation time.
items.bottom_line: Block deordering methods surpass MaxSAT optimization in automated planning by restructuring causal dependencies reliably.
